lessons.title: Nutrient needs of farm animals
lessons.html:
What livestock need from their feed

Feed is usually the biggest single cost in livestock production, and poor nutrition is behind many problems blamed on other causes: low conception rates, weak calves, slow growth and poor resistance to disease. A manager must understand what animals need and how to supply it at the lowest cost per kilogram of product.

The main nutrients

NutrientFunctionTypical sources
WaterEvery body function; the most important nutrientClean troughs, dams, boreholes
EnergyMaintenance, growth, milk, workGrazing, maize, molasses, hay
ProteinGrowth, milk, rumen microbesGreen grazing, lucerne, oilcake, licks with urea (ruminants only, as labelled)
MineralsBones, fertility, enzymes (e.g. phosphorus, calcium, salt, trace minerals)Mineral licks, salt
VitaminsHealth and fertilityGreen feed, supplements, injections on vet advice
FibreHealthy rumen function in ruminantsRoughage, hay, veld grass

Needs change with production stage

A dry cow in mid-pregnancy needs far less than the same cow in early lactation that must also conceive again. Growing weaners, ewes carrying twins and dairy cows in peak milk have the highest demands. Group animals by need and feed each group accordingly.

The seasonal feed gap

In summer-rainfall areas the veld is green and protein-rich in summer but becomes dry and low in protein in winter. Ruminants on dry veld therefore usually need a protein (winter) lick, while in summer a phosphorus (summer) lick is often required. Your feed supplier or animal nutritionist should formulate the programme for your farm.

Body condition scoring

Score animals regularly, using a scale such as 1 (very thin) to 5 (very fat), by feeling the backbone, ribs and tail-head. Body condition at mating and calving strongly affects fertility. Adjust feeding when the score drifts from the target.

lessons.title: Feeding programmes and safe feeding
lessons.html:
Putting the programme into practice

Building a feed budget

  1. Count animals in each group and estimate their daily needs.
  2. Estimate how much grazing is available in each camp and for how long.
  3. Plan supplementary feeds, licks, hay or silage to fill the gap.
  4. Price the options. Compare cost per unit of nutrient, not cost per bag.
  5. Store at least a reserve of roughage for drought.

Safe feeding rules

  • Change rations gradually over about a week or more. Sudden access to grain can cause acidosis, and sudden lush legumes can cause bloat.
  • Urea-containing licks are for ruminants only. Mix and feed exactly as the label says. Urea poisoning kills quickly; keep these licks dry and away from horses, pigs and poultry.
  • Provide enough trough space so timid animals also get their share.
  • Never feed mouldy feed. Store feed dry, off the floor, and protected from rodents.
  • Only use feeds registered under Act 36 of 1947 and follow withdrawal periods for medicated feeds.
  • Check water every day: troughs clean, ball valves working, no dead birds or algae.

Example

A 25 kg bag of protein lick costs R420 and one at R380 has a lower protein level. Calculate the cost per kilogram of protein for each before choosing. The cheaper bag may cost more for the nutrient you actually need.

Review the feed budget monthly. If grazing runs out sooner than planned, adjust early by buying feed, reducing numbers or moving animals, rather than waiting for animals to lose condition.

Record feed used per group.

lessons.title: Shelter and housing for livestock
lessons.html:
Protection from weather, predators and stress

Good shelter protects animals from cold, heat, wind, rain and predators, and makes handling easier. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes it an offence to keep animals in conditions that cause unnecessary suffering, including lack of shelter, water or food.

Requirements of good shelter

  • Space: enough room for all animals to lie down at the same time and move without injury.
  • Ventilation: fresh air without draughts at animal level; ammonia smell means poor ventilation or dirty bedding.
  • Drainage and flooring: dry, non-slip floors that slope to drains; no sharp edges.
  • Shade: trees or shade structures in hot areas, especially for pigs, dairy cows and feedlot cattle.
  • Protection from predators: secure night kraals for sheep and goats where jackals or caracal are a problem.
  • Easy cleaning: surfaces that can be scraped, washed and disinfected.

Special cases

  • Lambing and calving pens: clean, dry and sheltered, with good light for checking at night.
  • Sick pens: separate from healthy animals to limit disease spread.
  • Poultry and pigs: temperature control is critical for young animals; follow the breed or supplier management guide.

Maintenance routine

Inspect shelters weekly for broken boards, loose roof sheets, protruding nails and blocked drains. Remove manure regularly and compost it for the lands. Record repairs and costs so they can be budgeted.

Key points

  • Water is the most important nutrient; check it daily.
  • Match feeding to production stage and fill the seasonal feed gap with the right lick.
  • Change rations gradually; urea licks are for ruminants only and must follow the label.
  • Compare feeds on cost per unit of nutrient.
  • Shelter must give space, ventilation, drainage, shade and predator protection.
